tn.quote: QZ has four contrastive tones: high-rising (¹), high (²), low-rising (³), and low (⁴). ... 5.2 Tones All four tones are contrastive in words with simple vowels which are either open or end with a lenis consonant. ... High tone (²) and low tone (⁴) show no distributional restrictions and contrast with each other in many pairs. The low-rising tone (³) is found in all environments except on a simple vowel before a fortis consonant. The high-rising tone (¹) is by far the least common. It occurs only on simple vowels in open syllables or simple vowels followed by a lenis consonant.

529.quote: Word stress is always on the last syllable. In some contexts where isolated words are uttered in an imperative speech act, we may find the stress on the first syllable, e.g. déor ‘get out of here’ (‘outside’), dévan ‘in front!’ (call for the bus driver to stop at the next bus stop). Interestingly, there is no stress opposition as found in Mauritian Creole for synonyms as in réfer ‘do again’ vs. refér ‘recover from an illness’ (cf. Baker & Kriegel 2012, this volume). In Seychelles Creole both verbs with the two different meanings show the same stress pattern, i.e. stress on the last syllable.

tn.quote: Le tseltal n’étant en aucun cas une langue à tons, ni à accent intoné28, nous parlerons de tonalité vocalique plutôt que ton. ... On retiendra donc de ces mesures l’importance de normaliser les valeurs de F0, et la non incidence de la réarticulation et de la gémination sur le contour interne du noyau complexe – autrement dit, l’absence de corrélation tonale de ces réflexes.
tn.translation: Since Tseltal is in no way a tone language, nor a pitch-accent language, we will speak of vocalic tonality rather than tone. ... From these measurements we retain the importance of normalising F0 values, and the absence of any effect of rearticulation and gemination on the internal contour of the complex nucleus – in other words, the absence of a tonal correlation for these reflexes.

545.prule: Primary stress on the final vowel (last syllable) of the word; when a vowel-bearing suffix is added the stress moves onto it, so the suffixed word is again stressed on its last syllable. qtr.text: We agree with Mattos (1973, p. 2) that the stress pattern in Akwẽ-Xerente is predictable, hence post-lexical. tn.quote: Na seção 2.1.3 faz-se uma referência a Dixon (2010), quando descreve o acento como um dos sistemas prosódicos que se manifesta na sílaba da maioria das línguas que não possuem um sistema contrastivo de tom. Esse é também o caso do Akwẽ-Xerente, cujo acento tem sido qualificado de previsível (MATTOS, 1973), demarcativo e não-distintivo (BRAGGIO, 2005), e pós-lexical (SOUZA, 2008). A observação de palavras isoladas do corpus confirma, na maioria dos casos, o aspecto previsível do acento na língua, o qual recai geralmente sobre a última sílaba da palavra.
tn.translation: In section 2.1.3 reference is made to Dixon (2010), who describes stress as one of the prosodic systems manifested on the syllable in most languages that do not have a contrastive tone system. This is also the case of Akwẽ-Xerente, whose stress has been characterised as predictable (Mattos 1973), demarcative and non-distinctive (Braggio 2005), and post-lexical (Souza 2008). Observation of isolated words from the corpus confirms, in most cases, the predictable character of stress in the language, which generally falls on the last syllable of the word.
tn.cite: Frazão, Kêt Simas. 2013. A sílaba no Akwẽ-Xerente (Jê). Dissertação de Mestrado (Linguística), Universidade de Brasília. 127 pp. http://repositorio.unb.br/handle/10482/13857
tn.note: Not a tone language: the author places Akwẽ-Xerente among languages without a contrastive tone system; word prosody is predictable, non-distinctive stress, generally on the final syllable.
